\begin{abstract}
Latent world models that plan with short-horizon shooting become myopic
when the goal lies beyond one plan. We keep the official LeWorldModel
(LeWM) encoder, action-conditioned predictor, and 25-step
cross-entropy method (CEM) planner, and add two action-free imaginers
trained on detached latents. A forward map continues from the predicted
endpoint; a backward map walks the goal back toward it. Only the CEM
cost changes. We call this \emph{FaBLeWM} (Forward and Backward LeWM).
The imaginers are a longer-range ranking signal, not a claim that
$\Fk(p)$ recovers $z_{t+k}$. On PushT and TwoRoom ($n{=}50$, shared
starts, epoch-10 checkpoint, CEM horizon $5$), FaBLeWM matches Official
LeWM at goal offset $25$, where imagination is unused, and raises
success at offsets $50$--$100$. On TwoRoom, Official already reaches
$90\%$ at offset $25$ and then falls to $50/32/18$; Forward stays at
$90/84/66$.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

A learned latent world model is often paired with a short-horizon
planner. LeWorldModel~\citep{lewm2026} instantiates a joint-embedding
predictive architecture~\citep{lecun2022jepa} as an action-conditioned
world model: an encoder $E$ maps observations to latents, a predictor
$P$ rolls those latents forward under actions, and CEM~\citep{rubinstein1999cem}
selects a 25-step action sequence by the distance between the predicted
endpoint and a goal embedding. That loop is enough when the goal is
inside one planning horizon. It is not enough when the goal is $50$,
$75$, or $100$ steps away. CEM still emits 25-step plans; it ranks them
by how close a near-term endpoint sits to a still-distant goal.
Official success then drops, even if the same controller is reliable at
offset $25$.

Lengthening CEM is one response. We do not take it. We keep Official
LeWM---the encoder, the predictor, SIGReg, and the 25-step planner---and
change only the cost that ranks candidate plans. Two small action-free
networks, a forward imaginer $F$ and a backward imaginer $B$, are
trained on stop-gradient latents so that their losses cannot rewrite
$E$ or $P$. At evaluation, $F$ continues from the predicted endpoint
and $B$ walks the goal backward. When the remaining time to the goal
fits in one CEM plan, both maps are bypassed and the cost is exactly
Official. When it does not, CEM still plans 25 steps, but it scores
those steps with a longer-range view.

We call the method FaBLeWM (Forward and Backward LeWM). On PushT and
TwoRoom, with $50$ shared starts per task and the epoch-10 checkpoint,
the four modes coincide at offset $25$ and diverge later. On PushT,
Backward helps most at offset $50$ ($70\%$ vs.\ Official $44\%$) and
Forward is more stable at $75$ and $100$; a simple average of the two
costs is the strongest mid-range mix. On TwoRoom the bottleneck is
horizon mismatch rather than short-horizon competence: Official is
already at $90\%$ for offset $25$, then $50/32/18$. Forward recovers
$90/84/66$. A paired comparison at offset $50$ saves $21$ Official
failures and loses one success. We read this as ranking, not as
calibrated long-horizon prediction. Training diagnostics agree. On
PushT, $F$ and $B$ stay near the encoder's BatchNorm sphere; on
TwoRoom they do not, and Forward still helps.

\paragraph{Contributions.}
(i)~Detached forward and backward imaginers on an unchanged LeWM path.
(ii)~A CEM cost that applies $k$-step imagination only when the goal
lies beyond one plan, and reduces to Official when $k{=}0$.
(iii)~PushT and TwoRoom results in which longer-offset success rises
without a claim that $\Fk(p)\approx z_{t+k}$.

\section{Related work}
\label{sec:related}

Latent world models plan by imagining rollouts rather than by predicting
pixels. PlaNet~\citep{hafner2019planet} and Dreamer~\citep{hafner2020dreamer}
learn dynamics in a latent space; TD-MPC~\citep{hansen2022tdmpc} and
LeWM~\citep{lewm2026} score action sequences with CEM in that space.
All of these methods remain limited by the horizon of the shooter.
FaBLeWM does not replace LeWM's predictor with a longer action-conditioned
model. It adds action-free maps that change how a short CEM ranks
plans.

JEPA~\citep{lecun2022jepa} predicts in representation space.
LeWM is an action-conditioned JEPA world model with a Sketch Isotropic
Gaussian Regularizer (SIGReg) on the encoder. We take that model as
given. Inverse models that regress actions from pairs of states are a
different object: our backward imaginer is action-free and lives in
latent space. Hierarchical controllers that emit subgoals for a
lower-level policy are also different. $F$ and $B$ do not propose a
subgoal that another policy tracks; they re-score a flat 25-step CEM.
The baseline throughout is therefore Official LeWM with the same planner.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{Official LeWM}
\label{sec:official}

We use the official LeWM training path without modification. A window of
four encoded observations $z_{0:3}=E(o_{0:3})$ and the corresponding
actions is fed to $P$. There is no stop-gradient on prediction targets.
The loss is next-embedding MSE plus SIGReg,
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{official}}
=\underbrace{\|P(z,a)-z_{\mathrm{next}}\|^2}_{\mathrm{pred}}
+0.09\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SIGReg}}(z).
\end{equation}
At evaluation, CEM always plans $\planlen$ environment steps
(horizon $5$, receding horizon $5$, action block $5$). Official cost is
$\|\Pend-\zg\|^2$, where $\Pend$ is the predicted embedding after those
$25$ steps.

\subsection{Detached imaginers}
\label{sec:imaginers}

Forward $F$ and Backward $B$ are residual MLPs on a single latent.
They read stop-gradient copies of $z$ and $P$'s output $p$. Their
losses do not update $E$ or $P$. With a four-step window,
$p_1,p_2,p_3$ align with $z_1,z_2,z_3$.

\paragraph{Forward.}
$F$ is trained to map a predicted latent to a later encoder latent,
\begin{equation}
F(p_1)\to z_2,\qquad F(p_2)\to z_3,\qquad F(F(p_1))\to z_3,
\end{equation}
with equal weight on the one-step and two-step terms. At evaluation,
\begin{equation}
C_F=\bigl\|\Fk(\Pend)-\zg\bigr\|^2.
\end{equation}

\paragraph{Backward.}
The results in this paper use unary $B(z)\to z$:
\begin{equation}
B(z_3)\to z_2,\qquad B(z_2)\to z_1,\qquad B(B(z_3))\to z_1.
\end{equation}
At evaluation,
\begin{equation}
C_B=\bigl\|\Pend-\Bk(\zg)\bigr\|^2.
\end{equation}

\paragraph{Imagination depth.}
For goal offset $o$ and elapsed time $t$,
\begin{equation}
k=\max\bigl((o-t-\planlen)/5,\,0\bigr).
\end{equation}
The division by $5$ matches the action block, so $k$ counts imaginer
steps rather than environment steps. When $k{=}0$, $F$ and $B$ are
bypassed and $C_F=C_B=\|\Pend-\zg\|^2$. Offset $25$ at the first replan
has $k{=}0$, which is the sanity check that Official and the imaginer
modes must match.

\paragraph{Fusion.}
Unless noted, Fusion is a uniform mix
$C=0.5\,C_F+0.5\,C_B$ (avg05). CEM, the action space, and the 25-step
horizon are shared by Official, Forward, Backward, and Fusion.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:exp}

We evaluate four planning modes on the same frozen checkpoint: Official,
Forward, Backward, and Fusion (avg05). Each task uses $n{=}50$ episodes,
evaluation seed $42$, and a shared set of start states. Checkpoints are
taken at epoch $10$. CEM uses horizon $5$ at every offset. Success is
the environment's criterion, not latent MSE. PushT~\citep{florence2022ibc}
uses checkpoint \texttt{fblewm}; TwoRoom uses
\texttt{fblewm\_tworoom}. Both train unary $B\to z$.

\subsection{PushT}
\label{sec:pusht}

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{PushT success (\%). CEM horizon $5$ at all offsets. Same $50$ starts.
Checkpoint \texttt{fblewm}, unary $B\to z$.}
\label{tab:pusht}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
Mode & 25 & 50 & 75 & 100 \\
\hline \\
Official        & 82 & 44 & 22 & 12 \\
Forward         & 82 & 62 & 42 & 28 \\
Backward        & 82 & 70 & 34 & 10 \\
Fusion (avg05)  & 82 & 78 & 50 & 18 \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:pusht} is the main PushT result. At offset $25$ all four
modes are at $82\%$, as required by $k{=}0$. Gains appear once the goal
lies beyond one CEM plan. Backward is strongest at offset $50$
($+26$ points vs.\ Official). Forward is the better of the two unary
maps at offsets $75$ and $100$. Fusion is the best mid-range mix
($78\%$ and $50\%$ at offsets $50$ and $75$) and a small lift at
offset $100$ ($18\%$ vs.\ $12\%$). Offset $100$ remains hard.

Figure~\ref{fig:pusht-train} shows validation losses and latent norms.
SIGReg is calm from epoch $0$. By epoch $9$, Forward and Backward
outputs sit at about $13.0$ against encoder targets of about $13.8$,
near the BatchNorm sphere $\sqrt{192}\approx 13.9$. On this task the
imaginers can help while staying on the same scale as $E$.

\begin{figure}[t]
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_pusht_train.png}
\end{center}
\caption{PushT validation losses and latent norms over $10$ epochs.
Official is $\mathrm{pred}+0.09\cdot\mathrm{SIGReg}$. Forward and
Backward stay near the BatchNorm sphere
($\Vert z\Vert\approx\sqrt{192}\approx 13.9$).}
\label{fig:pusht-train}
\end{figure}

\subsection{TwoRoom}
\label{sec:tworoom}

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{TwoRoom success (\%). CEM horizon $5$ at all offsets. Same $50$ starts.
Checkpoint \texttt{fblewm\_tworoom}, unary $B\to z$.}
\label{tab:tworoom}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
Mode & 25 & 50 & 75 & 100 \\
\hline \\
Official        & 90 & 50 & 32 & 18 \\
Forward         & 90 & 90 & 84 & 66 \\
Backward        & 92 & 54 & 40 & 24 \\
Fusion (avg05)  & 90 & 76 & 58 & 32 \\
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_tworoom_success.png}
\end{center}
\caption{TwoRoom success (\%) vs.\ goal offset. Official LeWM uses
$25$-step CEM. Forward, Backward, and Fusion (avg05) keep that CEM and
change only the cost. Official is already strong at offset $25$ and
drops once the goal lies beyond one horizon; Forward recovers
long-offset success. Fusion does not beat Forward.}
\label{fig:tworoom-success}
\end{figure}

TwoRoom makes the horizon mismatch plain
(Table~\ref{tab:tworoom}, Figure~\ref{fig:tworoom-success}). Official
is already at $90\%$ for offset $25$, then $50/32/18$ at
$50/75/100$. Forward matches Official at offset $25$---the same five
episodes fail---and then stays at $90/84/66$. Relative to Official,
that is $+40$, $+52$, and $+48$ points. At offset $50$, a paired
count on the same starts is $21$ Official failures that Forward saves
and one Official success that Forward loses. Backward is a small lift
($+4$ to $+8$ points after offset $25$). Fusion sits between Forward
and Official; averaging in Backward hurts here.

This pattern is the opposite of ``the short-horizon controller is weak.''
The short-horizon controller is fine. What fails is ranking 25-step
plans against a goal that those plans cannot reach. Applying $\Fk$
before the distance to $\zg$ is a longer view of the same candidates,
not a new planner.

\begin{figure}[t]
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_tworoom_train.png}
\end{center}
\caption{TwoRoom validation losses and latent norms, including epochs
$0$--$1$. SIGReg spikes, then the encoder settles on the BatchNorm
sphere. Forward and Backward \emph{outputs} remain at about $5.6$
against targets of about $13.7$. Table~\ref{tab:tworoom} still holds:
ranking can survive a scale gap.}
\label{fig:tworoom-train}
\end{figure}

Figure~\ref{fig:tworoom-train} starts at epoch $0$. SIGReg is large in
the first two epochs ($61.5$ then $51.2$) and then falls as the encoder
moves onto the sphere; prediction MSE is not the quantity that
``recovers.'' After that, $F$ and $B$ outputs stay near $5.6$ while
their targets sit near $13.7$. We do not treat that gap as the cause of
the TwoRoom Forward gain, and we do not treat the PushT alignment as a
requirement either. Eval cost only has to order CEM samples.
PushT shows that F/B can help when norms are aligned; TwoRoom shows that
they can help when they are not. Neither plot is evidence that
$\Fk(p)$ is a calibrated forecast of $z_{t+k}$.

\subsection{Limitations of the present results}
\label{sec:limits}

The study is two tasks, one checkpoint time, and unary $B\to z$. PushT
at offset $100$ is still low. Fusion is not a universal improvement:
it is best on PushT at mid range and worse than Forward on TwoRoom.
We do not report other backward targets or further environments here.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:concl}

FaBLeWM leaves Official LeWM's encoder, predictor, and 25-step CEM in
place, and adds detached forward and backward imaginers that change how
that CEM ranks plans. On PushT and TwoRoom, the effect shows up where
it should: not at offset $25$, where $k{=}0$, but at longer offsets,
where a short planner is asked to choose among plans that do not reach
the goal. The working interpretation is a longer-range ranking signal,
not a calibrated long-horizon latent model.

\appendix
\section{Protocol details}
\label{app:protocol}

CEM uses \texttt{horizon=5}, \texttt{receding=5}, and
\texttt{action\_block=5}, so one plan is $\planlen$ environment steps.
Imagination depth is $k=\max((o-t-25)/5,\,0)$. Official cost is
$\|\Pend-\zg\|^2$; Forward is $\|\Fk(\Pend)-\zg\|^2$; unary Backward is
$\|\Pend-\Bk(\zg)\|^2$; Fusion (avg05) is the mean of the last two.
When $k{=}0$, Forward and Backward are skipped.

PushT starts hash:
\texttt{9d47d5e78eb0b98693bdb739e6e107fca7b52a7fa5d38189e418c242d7d2a703}.
TwoRoom starts hash:
\texttt{55d795562181c8f5eb12def43fb995cedd0d45c909fd1f39e38518155e16ad80}.

On TwoRoom at offset $50$, Forward vs.\ Official on the same $50$
starts: $21$ episodes saved, $1$ lost. Official and Forward at offset
$25$ fail on the same five episodes.
